meta.title: The E Form: Seventeen Notes, Four Frets
meta.summary: The E form is the only window whose whole scale fits inside four consecutive frets, with fret 11 sitting empty at the top — the one place in the chapter where a complete scale needs no shift at all.

spans.text: major on any string at all, and that was checked string by string — it's the only fret in the first twelve where that's true. Chapter 3 already noticed the pentatonic left it empty here, but a five-note scale skipping one fret barely counts as news. Now that all seven degrees are in play, the emptiness means something different: not a gap in an incomplete scale, but a genuine hole in the neck, one fret wide. Only two windows reach it at all — this one, at its top edge, and the D form, which is less lucky about where it lands. Every other fret between
carries something on at least two strings; this one carries nothing on any of them.

The consequence is the whole point of this lesson. Seventeen notes, four frets, one hand, nothing to shift for. No other window in this chapter manages that — the C form comes closest, but only because the nut plays two of its frets for free, and a fretting hand still has to cover the rest of it. If you're going to over-learn one window as a complete scale, this is the one. It's also the same window chapter 2 called the most-used barre on the instrument, and the one chapter 1 called the shape you navigate the rest of the neck from.
